chapters.category: Aramaic and Ethiopic textual traditions • Modern English research translation
chapters.title: Chapter 78 — The Names and Phases of the Sun and Moon
chapters.sourceNote: Translated afresh into clear modern English from the earliest primary-language witnesses responsibly available for this chapter. The Hasmonean-period Aramaic manuscript 4Q210 (4QEnastrᶜ ar), fragment 1 iii, is primary for its surviving lunar-fraction wording overlapping verses 6–8. The Aramaic manuscript 4Q209 (4QEnastrᵇ ar), especially fragment 26 and related lunar fragments, is primary for extant wording associated with the 177-day count and the moon's appearance in verses 15–17. Lacunae remain unsupplied. Proposed identifications of very small Greek P.Oxy. 2069 fragments with parts of this chapter are too slight and disputed to establish complete clauses. The complete Ethiopic (Geʽez) text in August Dillmann's 1851 critical edition, Liber Henoch Aethiopice, preserves all seventeen verses and supplies every portion not legible in Aramaic. Earlier legible Aramaic readings are followed where they correspond, while Geʽez preserves the complete sequence. No unattested wording was supplied, and no modern English translation was used as the translation base.

verses.text: The names of the sun are these: the first is Oryares, and the second is Tomas.
verses.study: The chapter begins by preserving two names for the sun. Naming marks the luminary as a known part of the revealed order.
crossReferences: Genesis 1:16 — the greater light is appointed to govern the day
Psalm 74:16 — day, night, moon and sun belong to God's ordering

verses.text: The moon has four names: its first name is Asonya, the second Ebla, the third Benase and the fourth Era.
verses.study: Four lunar names are recorded without explanation. Faithful transmission includes details whose full significance may remain unstated.
crossReferences: Psalm 8:3 — the moon is contemplated as the work of God's fingers
Psalm 104:19 — the moon is appointed for seasons

verses.text: These are the two great lights. Their circles are like the circle of heaven, and the measure of both is equal.
verses.study: The sun and moon are paired as great lights with matching circles in the vision's ancient model. The text emphasizes coordinated scale and order.
crossReferences: Genesis 1:16 — two great lights receive distinct rule
Sirach 43:2, 6 — sun and moon display ordered splendor

verses.text: In the sun's circle are seven portions of light beyond what is in the moon. Light is transferred to the moon by fixed measure until the seventh portion belonging to the sun has passed.
verses.study: Lunar light is described as measured transfer from the sun. The sevenfold reckoning makes increase accountable rather than vague.
crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 15:41 — sun and moon possess differing glory
James 1:17 — every good gift comes from the Father of lights

verses.text: They set and enter the western portals, circle by the north, and go out through the eastern portals across the face of heaven.
verses.study: Setting, circling and rising form one continuous route. The west, north and east portals belong to a single heavenly course.
crossReferences: Ecclesiastes 1:5 — the sun sets and hastens back to rise
Psalm 19:6 — the sun completes its circuit from end to end

verses.text: When the moon rises, one-fourteenth of its light appears in heaven and can be seen upon the earth. It increases each day until, on the fourteenth day, all its light is complete.
verses.study: The earliest surviving fractions describe visible light growing by fourteenths. Daily increase leads to a defined fullness.
crossReferences: Psalm 81:3 — the new moon and full moon mark appointed worship
Sirach 43:7–8 — the moon waxes wondrously and marks the months

verses.text: Fifteen portions of light are placed in it until the fifteenth day, when its light is complete as a sign for the year. It becomes fifteen portions, while the moon increases by one-fourteenth at a time.
verses.study: The chapter preserves both a fifteen-portion total and fourteenth-part increments. The ancient calculation is stated without forcing it into a later system.
crossReferences: Genesis 1:14 — the lights serve as signs for times and years
Psalm 90:12 — counted days train the heart in wisdom

verses.text: In its waning, on the first day the moon decreases to fourteen portions of light; on the second to thirteen; on the third to twelve; on the fourth to eleven; on the fifth to ten; on the sixth to nine; on the seventh to eight; on the eighth to seven; on the ninth to six; on the tenth to five; on the eleventh to four; on the twelfth to three; on the thirteenth to two; and on the fourteenth to half of one seventh. On the fifteenth day all the light that remains disappears completely.
verses.study: The descending count mirrors the earlier increase and carries the cycle to darkness. Each stage is preserved rather than summarized away.
crossReferences: Ecclesiastes 3:1 — every change has its appointed time
Jeremiah 31:35 — fixed ordinances govern sun, moon and stars

verses.text: In certain appointed months the moon has twenty-nine days, and at another time twenty-eight.
verses.study: Month lengths vary within the lunar reckoning. Difference is named as part of the law rather than treated as disorder.
crossReferences: 1 Chronicles 12:32 — understanding the times supports wise action
Colossians 2:16 — new moons belong to the calendar of appointed observance

verses.text: Uriel showed me another law: how light is placed in the moon and from which side the sun places it there.
verses.study: Uriel directs attention from the count to the source and side of illumination. Received wisdom includes both pattern and relation.
crossReferences: Daniel 1:17 — understanding of visions is given
Revelation 1:1 — angelic mediation communicates what is shown

verses.text: During the whole period in which the moon travels with its light, it adds light to itself opposite the sun. For fourteen days its light becomes complete in heaven, and when it is fully illuminated, all its light is complete in heaven.
verses.study: The moon's fullness is described through its position opposite the sun. The repeated completion stresses the visible culmination of the cycle.
crossReferences: Psalm 136:8–9 — sun and moon govern their appointed times
Isaiah 30:26 — intensified light becomes an image of restoration

verses.text: The first day is called the new moon, because on that day light rises upon it.
verses.study: The new moon is named at the first appearance of light. A small beginning marks the renewal of the whole cycle.
crossReferences: Numbers 28:11 — new moons receive appointed offerings
Isaiah 66:23 — worship is pictured from new moon to new moon

verses.text: It becomes exactly full on the day when the sun descends in the west and the moon rises from the east at night. The moon shines throughout the whole night until the sun rises opposite it, and the moon is seen opposite the sun.
verses.study: Fullness is identified by the opposing positions of sunset and moonrise. The night-long shining makes the relation observable.
crossReferences: Joshua 10:12–13 — sun and moon are named by their visible stations
Habakkuk 3:11 — sun and moon stand in their appointed place

verses.text: From the side where the moon's light comes out, there it begins to decrease again until all its light is gone. The days of the month pass, and its circle remains empty, without light.
verses.study: Waning begins from the side of illumination and continues to emptiness. Completion includes both fullness and the passing away of light.
crossReferences: Job 26:9 — the face of the full moon can be covered
Ecclesiastes 3:4 — seasons of fullness and loss alternate

verses.text: For three months it makes thirty days, and at its appointed time it makes three months of twenty-nine days. In these it completes its decrease during the first season and at the first portal, in 177 days.
verses.study: Six months combine three thirty-day and three twenty-nine-day months to total 177 days. The count ties lunar decrease to season and portal.
crossReferences: Genesis 8:13–14 — months and days are carefully counted
Daniel 8:14 — numbered periods are preserved with precision

verses.text: In the period of its going out, it appears for three months of thirty days each, and for three months it appears for twenty-nine days each.
verses.study: The six-month pattern is repeated in terms of appearance. Repetition verifies the alternation rather than adding a new total.
crossReferences: Genesis 1:14 — lights distinguish seasons, days and years
Psalm 104:19 — the moon governs appointed times

verses.text: At night it appears for twenty days at a time like a human figure, and by day it appears like heaven, for nothing is in it except its light.
verses.study: The final image compares the moon's night appearance to a human figure and its daytime appearance to heaven. The chapter closes by returning numerical instruction to visible form.
crossReferences: Psalm 89:37 — the moon is a faithful witness in the sky
1 Corinthians 15:40–41 — heavenly bodies possess their own splendor

explanation.heading: Chapter teaching and context
paragraphs: Chapter 78 names the sun and moon, describes their circles and presents lunar light as a measured relation to the sun. The ancient model is preserved on its own terms.
The moon's increase and decrease are counted in portions across fourteen- and fifteen-day stages. Fullness, waning and disappearance form a complete visible cycle.
Uriel's second law explains the moon's illumination, new moon and full moon through position and timing. Sunset in the west and moonrise in the east mark the point of fullness.
The final verses alternate thirty- and twenty-nine-day months and preserve a 177-day half-year count. Number, observation and transmitted instruction remain joined throughout the chapter.

crossReferences: Genesis 1:14–18 — the great lights mark signs, seasons, days and years
Psalm 19:1–6 — heavenly courses declare ordered glory
Psalm 81:3 — new moon and full moon mark appointed time
Psalm 104:19 — the moon is appointed for seasons
Jeremiah 31:35 — ordinances govern the heavenly lights
Sirach 43:2–8 — sun and moon display splendor and measure time
